title: SYSK Distraction Playlist: The Amazing History of Soda
summary: A distraction-playlist episode of Stuff You Should Know tracing the history of soda, from mineral water and early artificial carbonation (Priestley, Schweppe, Matthews, Plinth's siphon, Benjamin Silliman) through the rise of the soda fountain in pharmacies, the medicinal and drug-laced origins of sodas (including cocaine claims about Coca-Cola), flavored sodas, the soda fountain's link to bars and Prohibition and temperance, and its decline due to car culture and the bottle cap. Ends with listener mail from a teacher.

segments.title: Opening banter and soda fountain nostalgia
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the topic of soda and soda fountains, discuss regional terms for soft drinks, and joke about fifties nostalgia and Happy Days, then note soda fountains were already declining by the fifties.

segments.title: Mineral water and early carbonation
segments.summary: Hosts explain the appeal of naturally carbonated mineral water and its supposed health benefits, mention Pellegrino is artificially carbonated, and describe Joseph Priestley's 1767 experiment and Johann Jacob Schweppe's 1783 device.

segments.title: Sponsor reads
segments.summary: Sponsor reads for Stamps.com and a book recommendation for The Dorito Effect, plus a mention of a Shanon comedy podcast episode.

segments.title: Carbonation pioneers: Schweppe, Plinth, Mathews
segments.summary: Schweppe's process of making CO2 with sulfuric acid and marble and using cold water under pressure; Charles Plinth's perfected soda siphon; John Mathews's 1832 lead chamber generator that enabled soda fountains.

segments.title: Benjamin Silliman and early soda fountains
segments.summary: Yale chemistry professor Benjamin Silliman built two early soda fountains in New York City based on Mathews's design, serving carbonated water as medicine at the City Hotel and the Tontine Coffee House; he failed in business while others later built more successful shops.

segments.title: Soda fountains in pharmacies, soda jerks, and folk remedies
segments.summary: Soda fountains spread to pharmacies because pharmacists had the skill to make CO2 safely; soda jerks were skilled like bartenders. Root beer and small beer trace back to folk remedies and water purification, and pharmacies added drugs and alcohol to drinks.

segments.title: Phosphates and drugs in early soda
segments.summary: Phosphates, a popular fountain drink made with acid phosphate and fruit syrup, are described. Hosts discuss how early soft drinks contained alcohol and drugs such as cocaine, heroin, morphine, opium, and cannabis, before the Food and Drug Act of 1906.

segments.title: Sponsor read for Me Undies
segments.summary: Sponsor read for Me Undies underwear with a discount offer.

segments.title: Coca-Cola origins and cocaine claims
segments.summary: John Pemberton, a former Confederate colonel and pharmacist, created Coca-Cola in the 1880s in Atlanta, sold at Jacob's Pharmacy for a nickel; partner Frank Robinson named it and designed the script. Hosts discuss claims that it contained cocaine, which the company officially denies, and the contoured bottle. They also note Seven Up once contained lithium citrate.

segments.title: Flavored sodas, bars vs. soda fountains, and Prohibition
segments.summary: Early flavored sodas were citrus and other flavors, sold with cool-named syrups. Soda fountains resembled bars and competed with them; the temperance movement and Prohibition pushed people to soda shops, as argued in Ray Catherine Mayer's book Soda Shop Salvation.

segments.title: Decline of the soda fountain
segments.summary: Soda fountains numbered in the thousands and tens of thousands at their peak; they declined after the 1940s and 1950s. Causes given are car culture, suburbs, drive-through culture, and especially the bottle cap letting people drink soda at home.

segments.title: Listener mail: career change and teaching
segments.summary: A listener named Catherine (Mrs. Young) writes that the show's advice to do what you love helped her switch careers to teaching, and says she may use the show in her classroom.

segments.title: Outro and contact info
segments.summary: Hosts give social media and email contact information and the website, and sign off.
